title: Chapter 38 — Conclusion
paragraphs: Reader, I married him. A quiet wedding we had—just he and I, the parson, and the clerk. When we got back from church, I went into the kitchen of the manor house, where Mary was cooking dinner and John cleaning the knives, and I said—

"Mary, I married Mr. Rochester this morning." The housekeeper and her husband were both the kind of calm, steady people to whom you can safely announce remarkable news without having your ears pierced by a shriek or your head stunned by a flood of amazed chatter. Mary did look up, and she did stare at me. The ladle she was using to baste a pair of roasting chickens did stop in midair for about three minutes. Then, without comment, she resumed her basting. When she had finished and put the ladle down, she said—
"Have you, Miss? Well, I never!"

A short time later she added: "I saw you go out with the master, but I didn't know you'd gone to church to be married." And she went back to her basting. John, when I turned to him, was grinning from ear to ear.

"I told Mary how it would be," he said. "I knew what Mr. Edward"—John was an old servant who had known his master since boyhood, so he often used his first name—"I knew what Mr. Edward would do. And I was certain he wouldn't wait long either. And he's done right, in my opinion. I wish you joy, Miss!" And he politely touched his forehead.

"Thank you, John. Mr. Rochester told me to give you and Mary this." I pressed a five-pound note into his hand. Without waiting to hear more, I left the kitchen. Passing the door a short while later, I caught the words—

"She'll likely do better for him than any of the grand ladies would have." And again: "If she's not one of the handsomest, she's no fool and very good-natured. And in his eyes she's beautiful—anyone can see that."

I wrote to Moor House and to Cambridge immediately, explaining what I had done and fully laying out my reasons. Diana and Mary approved the step without reservation. Diana announced she would give me time to finish the honeymoon, and then she would come and see me.

"She'd better not wait that long, Jane," said Mr. Rochester when I read her letter to him. "If she does, she'll be too late—for our honeymoon will last our whole lives. Its light will only fade over your grave or mine."

How St. John received the news, I don't know. He never answered the letter in which I told him. Yet six months later he wrote to me—without, however, mentioning Mr. Rochester's name or my marriage. His letter was calm and, though very serious, kind. He has kept up a regular, if not frequent, correspondence ever since. He hopes I am happy and trusts I am not among those who live without God in the world and think only of earthly things.

You haven't quite forgotten little Adele, have you, reader? I hadn't. I soon asked and received permission from Mr. Rochester to visit her at the school where he had placed her. Her wild joy at seeing me again moved me deeply. She looked pale and thin. She said she was unhappy. I found the school's rules were too strict and its coursework too demanding for a child her age. I took her home with me. I had planned to be her governess again, but soon realized that was impractical. So I found a school with a more relaxed approach and placed her there. She settled in well, made good progress, and eventually grew into a pleasant and kind young woman. A good education corrected whatever flaws her French upbringing had given her, and when she left school I found her a faithful and agreeable companion.
My story draws near its close. One word about my experience of married life, and one brief glance at the fortunes of those whose names have appeared most often in this narrative, and I am done.

I have now been married ten years. I know what it is to live entirely for and with the person I love most on earth. I consider myself supremely blessed—blessed beyond what words can express—because I am my husband's life as fully as he is mine. No woman was ever nearer to her husband than I am. We are truly bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh. I never tire of my Edward's company. He never tires of mine, any more than we each tire of the heartbeat in our own chests. We are always together. To be together is for us to be at once as free as if we were alone, and as content as if we were in company. We talk all day long. To talk to each other is only a more animated and audible form of thinking. His presence is all I need. Mine, he says, is all he needs.

Mr. Rochester continued to be blind for the first two years of our marriage. Perhaps it was that circumstance that drew us so close—that bound us so tightly. For I was his eyes, as I am still his right hand. Literally, I was—as he often called me—the apple of his eye. He saw nature and books through me. I never tired of gazing on his behalf and putting into words what I saw—field, tree, town, river, cloud, sunbeam. The landscape before us, the weather around us. And impressing by sound on his ear what light could no longer stamp upon his eyes.
One morning, at the end of those two years, as I was writing a letter to his dictation, he came and bent over me and said: "Jane, have you a glittering ornament around your neck?"
I had a gold watch chain. I answered "Yes."
"And have you a pale blue dress on?"
And have you a pale blue dress on?
I had. He told me then that for some time he had thought the darkness clouding one eye was becoming less dense. Now he was sure of it.

He and I went to London. He consulted an eminent eye specialist and eventually recovered the sight of that one eye. He cannot see very clearly now. He cannot read or write much. But he can find his way without being led by the hand. The sky is no longer a blank to him—the earth no longer a void. When his firstborn was placed in his arms, he could see that the boy had inherited his own eyes, as they once were—large, brilliant, and dark. On that occasion, he acknowledged once more, with deep gratitude: "God is merciful! He sees that I have earned the right to a little happiness, and He grants it."

My Edward and I are happy. And the more so because those we love most are happy too. Diana and Mary Rivers are both married. They visit us once a year, and we visit them. Diana's husband is a captain in the navy—a brave officer and a good man. Mary's is a clergyman, a college friend of her brother's, and worthy of the connection in every respect. Both Captain Fitzjames and Mr. Wharton love their wives and are loved by them.

As for St. John Rivers, he left England. He went to India. He entered on the path he had chosen for himself, and he follows it still. A more determined, tireless pioneer never struggled through hardship and danger. Firm, faithful, and devoted, full of energy, zeal, and truth, he works for humanity. He clears their painful way toward progress. He cuts down prejudices of creed and caste like a giant felling trees. He may be stern. He may be demanding. He may be ambitious still. But his is the sternness of the warrior who guards his captain's tent. His is the ambition of the servant laboring in his Master's vineyard. He is a man willing to lay down his life for the truth.

St. John is unmarried. He never will marry now. He has been enough, by himself, for the work. And the work draws near its end. His glorious sun is hastening toward its setting. The last letter I received from him drew human tears from my eyes yet filled my heart with divine joy. He anticipated his sure reward—his imperishable crown. I know that a stranger's hand will write to me next, to say that the good and faithful servant has been called at last into the joy of his Lord. And why weep for this? No fear of death will darken St. John's last hour. His mind will be unclouded, his heart will be unshaken, his hope will be sure, his faith will be steadfast. His own words are a pledge of this—
"My Master," he says, "has forewarned me. Daily He announces more distinctly—'Surely I come quickly!' and hourly I more eagerly respond—'Amen; even so, come, Lord Jesus!'"
